concept.name: Consistency Models & Replication Guarantees

relationships.description: Connects latency-vs-consistency trade-offs to concrete client consistency guarantees.
Shows how R + W > N quorums interact with linearizability and read repair.

concept.tagline: Why a user refreshes their profile right after saving and sees stale data—and how linearizability, causal ordering, and read-your-writes session tokens prevent phantom regressions.
concept.purpose: Choose the weakest consistency model that preserves application invariants without paying global consensus latency on every read.

prerequisites.title: Replication Lag & Follower Reads
prerequisites.summary: Asynchronous read replicas trail the primary WAL by milliseconds to seconds, causing stale reads unless routed or fenced.

prerequisites.title: Real-Time Ordering vs. Causal Ordering
prerequisites.summary: Linearizability enforces a single global real-time order across all operations; causal consistency orders only causally related events while allowing concurrent unrelated writes to proceed without cross-region locks.

spark.summary: Routing writes to a primary database and reads to asynchronous replicas causes users to save a password or post a comment and immediately see their old state on refresh. Defaulting to full linearizability for every endpoint adds cross-AZ or cross-region quorum RTT to every read, whereas matching each workflow to Read-Your-Writes session tokens, Monotonic Reads, Causal Consistency, or Linearizability preserves correctness at a fraction of the latency cost.
spark.keyTakeaway: When choosing consistency levels across replicated storage, reserve strict linearizability for uniqueness constraints, leader leases, and financial balances, while using Read-Your-Writes session tokens or causal consistency for user-facing feeds and profiles so reads scale horizontally without stale regressions.
spark.byteSummary:
Distributed consistency is not a binary choice between 'strong' and 'broken'. Under asynchronous replication, three distinct user-visible anomalies appear: stale reads after your own write, time-traveling backward when consecutive reads hit replicas at different replication offsets, and out-of-order replies where an answer appears before its question.

Read-Your-Writes consistency solves self-edits cheaply by tracking the writer's monotonic WAL LSN or version token and routing subsequent reads to a replica caught up to at least that offset. Causal consistency tracks vector clocks or dependency tokens across threads so replies never precede parent posts, without paying cross-region consensus latency.

Reserve Linearizability (single global real-time order via Raft/Paxos quorums and read-index leases) for invariants where two concurrent actors cannot both win—such as distributed locks, username claims, and account debits.

learningJourney.title: The Three Anomalies That Break Asynchronous Read Replicas
learningJourney.purpose: Trace Read-Your-Writes violations, Monotonic Read regressions, and Causal inversions in production.

explanation.foundation: Suppose Primary DB commits `UPDATE users SET bio = 'Staff Eng'` at WAL LSN `1042`, and Replica A is at LSN `1038` (12 ms behind) while Replica B is at LSN `1042`. When the user reloads their profile 5 ms later and hits Replica A, their new bio vanishes.
explanation.core:
Three concrete consistency guarantees eliminate these anomalies without global consensus:
1. **Read-Your-Writes (RYW)**: A user always sees mutations they themselves submitted, even if other users briefly see older data.
2. **Monotonic Reads**: Once a user observes state at LSN `1042`, subsequent reads for that user never route to a replica behind LSN `1042` (preventing 'time travel' when load balancers bounce requests between Replica B and Replica A).
3. **Causal Consistency**: If Event B happens after observing Event A (e.g., Alice posts a bug, Bob replies 'Fixed'), every observer sees A before B, while concurrent unrelated posts can arrive in any order.
explanation.deepDive: **Why R+W > N Alone Is Not Linearizable**: Even in a Dynamo-style quorum store with $N=3, W=2, R=2$, two concurrent reads during a partial write propagation can return the new value to Reader 1 and the old value to Reader 2 unless read-repair blocks before returning—violating linearizability. learningJourney.title: From Eventual to Linearizable: Cost vs. Invariant Strength
learningJourney.purpose: Compare latency, availability under partition, and invariant guarantees across the consistency spectrum.

explanation.foundation: Stronger consistency restricts which replicas can answer a read and how many nodes must acknowledge a write—directly trading tail latency and partition availability for global ordering.
explanation.core:
- **Eventual Consistency**: Replicas converge once writes stop; reads serve locally in `< 1 ms` from any node. Great for view counters, recommendations, and DNS.
- **Causal Consistency**: Tracks causal dependencies (`context_token`); commits locally in one datacenter (`< 5 ms`) and replicates causally across regions without cross-ocean consensus.
- **Sequential Consistency**: All nodes observe operations in the same global order, though not necessarily matching wall-clock timestamps.
- **Linearizability (Strong Consistency)**: Every operation appears to take effect atomically at a single point between its invocation and response. Requires Raft/Paxos quorum writes and leader lease or quorum reads.
explanation.deepDive: **Strict Serializability vs. Linearizability**: Linearizability governs single-object real-time ordering; Serializability governs multi-object ACID transaction isolation without real-time constraints. Combining both yields **Strict Serializability** (e.g., Google Spanner TrueTime, CockroachDB), the strongest practical model.

learningJourney.title: LSN-Bounded Replica Router for Read-Your-Writes in Java
learningJourney.purpose: Implement a session-token LSN router that serves from fast read replicas whenever caught up, falling back to primary only when replica lag exceeds the caller's write offset.

explanation.foundation: Sticky routing to the primary for 5 seconds after every write works for low write rates, but write-heavy users pin all their reads onto the primary. Tracking the exact monotonic WAL LSN (`pg_current_wal_lsn()`) lets any replica that has replayed `>= minRequiredLsn` serve the read immediately.
explanation.deepDive: Store `sessionMinLsn` in a signed HTTP-only cookie or Redis session key (`user:{id}:min_lsn`), advancing it monotonically via `Math.max(existingLsn, newCommitLsn)` so Monotonic Reads and Read-Your-Writes both hold simultaneously.

learningJourney.title: Cross-Region Causal Tokens vs. Synchronous Quorum Latency
learningJourney.purpose: Evaluate multi-region consistency trade-offs under speed-of-light RTT constraints.

explanation.foundation: Across US-East and EU-West (~75 ms RTT), linearizable quorum writes require at least one cross-ocean round trip (~80–120 ms p99). For collaborative comments, social feeds, or shopping carts, paying 100 ms per click hurts conversion.
explanation.core: Causal consistency (used in systems like Meta's TAO / Lamport-clock replication pipelines) attaches a compact causal dependency token to writes. Local datacenters acknowledge writes in `< 5 ms`, and remote regions buffer out-of-order replicated events until their causal parent LSN arrives.
explanation.deepDive: **When NOT to Use Weak/Causal Consistency**: Never use eventual or causal consistency for inventory decrement below zero, distributed lock acquisition, unique handle registration, or account balance debits—two concurrent writers in different regions would both succeed and violate the invariant.

decisionFramework.problem: How to guarantee users immediately see their own profile/settings updates while still offloading 90%+ of reads to asynchronous replicas.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Route all reads for every user to the primary database, or enable linearizable quorum reads globally.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Routing all reads to the primary defeats read-replica horizontal scaling and saturates primary CPU/IOPS.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare primary-only reads, fixed 5-second sticky-primary cookies, and LSN-tracked replica routing.
decisionFramework.decision: Propagate the monotonic commit LSN in the user's session token and route reads to any healthy replica whose `applied_lsn >= session_min_lsn`, falling back to the primary only when all replicas lag behind.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Preserves Read-Your-Writes and Monotonic Reads while offloading >95% of reads to replicas within milliseconds of commit.

decisionExercise.prompt: In a multi-region comment system, Alice in US-East posts a question (`msg_1`), and Bob in US-East posts a reply (`msg_2` referencing `msg_1`). Carol in EU-West loads the thread and sees Bob's reply (`msg_2`) before Alice's question (`msg_1`) has replicated to EU-West. Which consistency guarantee was violated, and what is the lowest-latency fix?

options.label: Monotonic Reads was violated; force all EU-West reads to query the US-East primary synchronously.
options.explanation: Cross-ocean reads add ~80 ms RTT to every page load when causal dependency tracking solves it locally.

options.label: Causal Consistency was violated; attach `parent_lsn` (`msg_1`) to `msg_2` so EU-West holds `msg_2` from visibility until `msg_1` is applied.
options.explanation: Causal consistency ensures causally dependent events appear in order without cross-region consensus latency.

options.label: Read-Your-Writes was violated; give Carol a sticky session to US-East.
options.explanation: Carol did not write either message; she is observing a causal relationship between Alice's and Bob's writes.

learningJourney.title: Clock Skew Pitfalls, Replica Stall Edge Cases & Glossary
learningJourney.purpose: Highlight subtle failure modes in session-LSN routing and define canonical consistency terms.

explanation.foundation:
**Edge Cases & Failure Modes**:
- **Replica Lag Spike Fallback Storm**: If network congestion causes all replicas to lag 10 seconds behind the primary, LSN-aware routing falls back 100% of active writers onto the primary. Pair fallback with a circuit breaker or bounded wait (e.g., wait up to 15 ms for a replica to catch up before hitting primary).
- **Wall-Clock Timestamp Trap**: Never compare `updated_at` wall-clock timestamps from different app nodes to resolve conflicts (Last-Writer-Wins); NTP clock skew can silently discard newer writes.
explanation.core:
**Assumptions & Glossary**:
- **Assumptions**: Assumes single-leader WAL replication exposes a monotonically increasing sequence number (`LSN` or `GTID`) per shard.
- **Linearizability**: Strongest single-object consistency; every read returns the value of the most recent completed write in real time.
- **Causal Consistency**: Operations that are causally related are seen by every node in the same order; concurrent operations may be seen in different orders.
- **Read-Your-Writes**: Session guarantee ensuring a client always observes its own prior updates.
explanation.deepDive: Matching the consistency guarantee to each endpoint's true invariant keeps systems both fast and bug-free.

knowledgeChecks.question: A user updates their shipping address and immediately refreshes the page. On refresh 1 they see the new address, and on refresh 2 (routed to a different read replica) they see the old address. Which consistency guarantee is violated?

options.feedback: Correct: bouncing between a caught-up replica and a lagging replica causes time-traveling backward (violating Monotonic Reads) and hides the user's own write (violating Read-Your-Writes).
No locks are blocked; this is a replication visibility anomaly.
Foreign keys are intact; the two replicas are simply at different WAL offsets.
Neither replica is malicious; one simply lags behind the primary WAL.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Monotonic Reads prevents a user from observing older state after already observing newer state.

knowledgeChecks.question: How does LSN-aware read routing preserve Read-Your-Writes without forcing all reads onto the primary database?

options.feedback: Replication remains asynchronous; the router simply checks replica progress.

options.text: It records the user's latest commit WAL LSN in their session and routes reads to any healthy replica whose `applied_lsn >= session_min_lsn`.
options.feedback: Correct: once a replica replays past `session_min_lsn`, it can safely serve the user's reads.

options.text: It flushes Redis cache on every SELECT query.
options.feedback: Cache flushing does not advance a lagging database replica.

options.text: It uses client wall-clock timestamps to pick replicas.
options.feedback: Client clocks are untrusted and skewed relative to database WAL positions.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Comparing monotonic WAL LSNs provides an exact mathematical condition for replica freshness.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which workload strictly requires Linearizability rather than Causal or Eventual consistency?

options.text: Incrementing a public video view counter
options.feedback: Approximate eventual counters (CRDTs/batched increments) are far cheaper and sufficient.

options.text: Claiming a globally unique username or acquiring a distributed leader lease
options.feedback: Correct: two concurrent requests cannot both claim the same unique handle or hold the same exclusive lease; a single global real-time order is mandatory.
Newsfeeds tolerate eventual or causal ordering.
Read-heavy catalogs thrive under eventual caching.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Uniqueness constraints and mutual exclusion require linearizable consensus.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is Causal Consistency lower-latency across regions than Linearizability?

options.text: Because causal consistency never replicates data across regions.
options.feedback: It replicates asynchronously across regions while tracking causal parent dependencies.

options.text: Causal consistency allows concurrent unrelated operations to commit locally without cross-region quorum coordination, ordering only causally dependent events.
options.feedback: Correct: avoiding cross-ocean quorum RTT on every write keeps local write latency in single-digit milliseconds.

options.text: Because causal consistency drops all writes during network partitions.
options.feedback: Causal consistency remains available for local writes during partitions (AP/Causal+).

options.text: Because it stores all data in browser localStorage.
options.feedback: Causal tokens are lightweight metadata vectors/LSNs exchanged between clients and servers.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Causal consistency is the strongest consistency model achievable in an Available, Partition-Tolerant (AP) system.

beginner.summary: When a database copies writes from a primary server to read replicas, there is a slight delay. Consistency models define what promises the system makes during that delay—such as 'Read-Your-Writes' (you always see your own edits) versus 'Linearizability' (everyone sees everything in exact real-time order).
beginner.keyTakeaway: When using read replicas, track the user's latest write version so their own reads never hit a lagging replica, and save expensive global consensus for critical operations like payments or unique usernames.
beginner.byteSummary: Imagine saving your profile picture and refreshing the page, only to see your old picture because your second request hit a slower backup copy of the database. By tagging your session with the version number of your save, the router knows to send your reads only to copies that have caught up.

intermediate.summary: Match consistency models to endpoint invariants: use LSN-aware replica routing for Read-Your-Writes and Monotonic Reads, dependency watermarks for Causal Consistency, and Raft/Paxos quorums with leader leases for Linearizability.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When choosing consistency levels across replicated storage, reserve strict linearizability for uniqueness constraints, leader leases, and financial balances, while using Read-Your-Writes session tokens or causal consistency for user-facing feeds and profiles so reads scale horizontally without stale regressions.
intermediate.byteSummary: Strong consistency is expensive because it forces coordination across replicas on the critical path. Tracking monotonic WAL LSNs per user session offloads >95% of reads to replicas while eliminating stale self-reads, whereas causal consistency prevents out-of-order comment threads across regions without cross-ocean quorum RTT.

advanced.summary: Distinguish single-object Linearizability from transactional Strict Serializability, understand why naive R + W > N quorums without synchronous read-repair fail linearizability, and guard LSN-aware routers against primary fallback stampedes during replica lag spikes.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When operating replicated storage at scale, pair LSN-bounded replica routing with bounded catch-up waits and circuit breakers so sudden replica lag spikes do not stampede all read traffic onto the primary.
advanced.byteSummary: Even quorum systems (R + W > N) violate linearizability if concurrent readers observe partial write propagation before read-repair completes. In leader-follower topologies, LSN-tracked routing must cap primary fallback concurrency during network brownouts so a lagging replica fleet does not take down the primary.
